publisher: Boston University Global Development Policy Center
title: Geopolitics on the Rise, IMF on the Decline: Insights from the Updated Global Financial Safety Net Tracker
date_evidence: meta-last-updated: 2026-02-17 ; 'Posted 4 months ago on Monday, January 26th, 2026'.
key_claim: The January 2026 GFSN Tracker records 19 bilateral currency-swap arrangements in 2025 with total swap volume of $517 billion, up from $111 billion in 2024 and $93 billion in 2023; the People's Bank of China has signed over 80 contracts since 2020, the United States offered a $20 billion swap to Argentina, and while IMF unconditional lending facilities since the pandemic total $273 billion against $190 billion of conditional lending, a recent Executive Board decision will cut unconditional crisis finance such as the RCF and RFI back toward 100 percent of quota from 2027, so safety nets are becoming more multipolar and more unequal.
frame_summary: The authors argue the global financial safety net is decentralising into a multipolar, increasingly unequal patchwork in which bilateral swaps and regional arrangements rival the IMF, leaving the poorest countries with the least reliable access.
notes: Structural anchor (Jan 2026, 3-6m band, within 12 months). Core quantitative spine: $517bn, $111bn, $93bn, $20bn, $273bn, $190bn.

title: Introductory Remarks at the IMF's Middle East and Central Asia Department Press Briefing
date_evidence: Jihad Azour, Director, Middle East and Central Asia Department, April 2026 Regional Economic Outlook Update — 'April 16, 2026'.
key_claim: Since the pandemic the IMF has approved nearly $46 billion in financing for the Middle East and Central Asia region, with key active programmes including Egypt's Extended Fund Facility of about $8.1 billion, Pakistan's EFF of $7.2 billion, Morocco's Flexible Credit Line of $4.8 billion and Jordan's four-year EFF of $1.2 billion, while sovereign spreads for oil importers widened by 50 to 100 basis points during March before retreating after the ceasefire.
frame_summary: The IMF presents itself as the standing, scalable backstop for the region, ready to scale up financing and policy support as the conflict shock unfolds.
notes: Tier 1, shows the IMF/Western track still large and active; $46bn, Egypt $8.1bn, Pakistan $7.2bn, Morocco $4.8bn, Jordan $1.2bn.

title: Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable - 6th Co-Chairs Progress Report
date_evidence: Press release — 'Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable - 6th Co-Chairs Progress Report — April 15, 2026'.
key_claim: The Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable, co-chaired by the IMF, the World Bank and the G20 presidency and convening debtor countries, Paris Club and new bilateral creditors and private creditors, issued an updated Restructuring Playbook, a Liability Management Operations Manual and a set of common understandings to improve restructuring processes and timelines.
frame_summary: The official multilateral track is responding to fragmented creditor coordination by building shared procedural tools and common understandings among traditional, new and private creditors rather than a binding mechanism.

title: Central Bank Currency Swaps Tracker
key_claim: Since 2009 China has signed bilateral currency-swap agreements with over 40 counterparties, and the People's Bank of China uses swaps largely as a substitute for collateralised lending to heavily indebted countries, with more than three-quarters of partners drawing on them for balance-of-payments support and Pakistan's annual draw rising from $820 million to $4.3 billion in 2025 to finance external debt owed largely to Chinese institutions.
frame_summary: CFR argues the PBoC swap network is a structurally different, opaque form of de facto long-term balance-of-payments lending that often refinances debt owed to Chinese institutions, distinct from the Fed and ECB crisis-liquidity model.
notes: Tier 2 on the China swap track; Pakistan $820 million to $4.3 billion.

title: China Is Building New Financial Architecture for Clean Energy Tech. It May Come with Conditions.
key_claim: The People's Bank of China had thirty-two active bilateral swap agreements in May 2025, and these renminbi corridors are assembling into a finance-plus-technology offer for the Global South, illustrated by Nigeria's RMB 15 billion ($2.5 billion) swap and Kenya's conversion of $3.5 billion of dollar loans into fixed-rate renminbi loans saving over $200 million a year, an offer that arrives with conditionality and sovereignty risks Western programmes do not impose.
frame_summary: Carnegie argues China is building a parallel, renminbi-denominated and increasingly programmable financial architecture for the Global South that the West cannot match on scale or cost, but that carries embedded conditionality.
notes: Tier 2, most recent (16/06/2026); Nigeria RMB 15 billion / $2.5 billion, Kenya $3.5 billion, $200 million.

title: IMF-World Bank Spring Meetings 2026: What We're Watching
date_evidence: by Rachel Glennerster, Nancy Lee, et al. — 'April 13, 2026'.
key_claim: CGD experts note that in 2025 African governments spent nearly a fifth of their revenues on interest and four out of five spent more on debt service than on health or education, that IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva says near-term demand for IMF finance could reach $50 billion and World Bank President Ajay Banga is discussing $20-$25 billion in rapid financing, and they ask what role other creditors, bilateral such as China and private, will play as fragmentation intensifies.
frame_summary: CGD argues the Western multilateral institutions are straining to meet crisis demand within tight concessional envelopes, raising the question of which other creditors fill the gap as the system fragments.

title: On the Safe-haven Status of the US Dollar
date_evidence: meta-dc.date: 2026-03-07 ; Andrew Hauser, Deputy Governor, speech.
key_claim: Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser argues that, despite diversification, the US dollar remains close to half of all official reserves, US foreign-exchange and Treasury markets remain by far the most liquid traditional safe havens, foreigners remain large net buyers of US assets, and observed shifts in reserves and hedging are glacial, with change coming not with a bang but by degree.
frame_summary: Hauser argues the predicted erosion of dollar and US-system dominance is far slower and less dramatic than headlines imply, a counter to claims of a rapidly fragmenting post-dollar safety net.
verbatim_quote: not with a bang, but by degree
notes: Tier 1 counter-argument source on dollar dominance.
